summary: This Wikipedia article covers the Aesop fable 'The Fox and the Grapes' (Perry Index 15), in which a fox that cannot reach grapes declares them sour or unripe, giving rise to the idiom 'sour grapes'. It traces the fable's retellings by Phaedrus, La Fontaine, Babrius and others, discusses its psychological reading as cognitive dissonance, lists concise English translations, and surveys its artistic uses in furniture, porcelain, tiles, medallions and musical settings, plus its spread into other languages with variants such as cherries or rowanberries.
one_line: Wikipedia article on Aesop's fable of the fox who calls unreachable grapes sour, its many retellings, artworks, and the 'sour grapes' idiom.
key_facts: The Fox and the Grapes is one of Aesop's Fables, numbered 15 in the Perry Index.
The story concerns a fox that tries to eat grapes from a vine but cannot reach them, and then states they are undesirable.
The expression 'sour grapes' originated from this fable.
The fable is one of the few that feature only a single animal protagonist.
Phaedrus's Latin version (IV.3) ends with the fox remarking 'Oh, you aren't even ripe yet! I don't need any sour grapes.'
La Fontaine's French version (III.11), Le Renard et les Raisins, is almost as concise and pointed as the early versions of Babrius and Phaedrus.
Pierre Julien's statue of La Fontaine, commissioned in 1782, is now in the Louvre and includes a fox seated at the poet's feet.
Peter Abelard said in the 12th century that a version in which the fox is after cherries had become proverbial.
In the Scandinavian version the fox complains about rowanberries, since grapes are not common in northern latitudes.
Aphra Behn's quatrain appeared in Francis Barlow's illustrated edition of the fables (1687).
W. J. Linton reduced the fable to a limerick for Walter Crane's Baby's Own Aesop (1887), with the moral 'The grapes of disappointment are always sour'.
Jon Elster calls the pattern of mental behaviour in the fable 'adaptive preference formation'.
Jean-Baptiste Oudry's series based on La Fontaine's fables was produced by the Beauvais and Gobelins tapestry works during the 1740s.
Martin Jugiez (d. 1815) had a workshop in Philadelphia where a Fox and Grapes chest of drawers was produced.
Isaac de Benserade summed up the fable in a quatrain accompanying the hydraulic statue of it in the labyrinth of Versailles.
